# Part A — the CPU waits for memory {style="text-align: center;"}

## The memory hierarchy

- Add two floats: **< 1 ns**. Fetch from RAM: **~100 ns**.

. . .

| Level | Size | Latency | If L1 = 1 s |
|---|---|---|---|
| registers | ~100s B | ~0 | instant |
| **L1** | 32–64 KB / core | ~1 ns | 1 s |
| **L2** | 256 KB–1 MB | ~4 ns | 4 s |
| **L3** | 8–32 MB | ~15 ns | 15 s |
| **RAM** | 16–64 GB | ~100 ns | **~2 min** |

::: {.notes}
While waiting, the core could have done hundreds of operations.
This machine: L1d 544 KiB total (14 instances), L2 18 MiB (9 instances), L3 24 MiB
shared. Hybrid CPU (P/E/LP-E cores) — per-core L1 differs, hence "instances".
`lscpu` shows it; the script asks students to compare with their own.
:::

## Caches bet on locality

- **Temporal**: used now → used again soon.
- **Spatial**: used now → **neighbors** next.
- Memory moves in **lines** of 64 B = 8 Float64.

. . .

> Fast code [**honors that bet**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

## Bet before you look 🎲 {style="text-align: center;"}

. . .

Sum the **same array** many times, from **8 KB to 64 MB**.

. . .

L1 ≈ 1 ns, RAM ≈ 100 ns.

. . .

> ### How much slower per access at 64 MB?

. . .

> *(~100×? Write it down.)*

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "1. The memory hierarchy — the cache cliff"

## The cache cliff, measured

. . .

```julia
for _ in 1:passes                 # repeated_sum(a, passes)
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(a)
        s += a[i]
    end
end
```

. . .

| footprint | ns / access | lives in |
|---|---|---|
| 8 KB | **0.049** | L1 |
| 4 MB | **0.128** | L2 (18 MiB) |
| 64 MB | **0.317** | RAM (> 24 MiB L3) |

. . .

> Steps visible. But [**6.5×, not ~100×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Why?

::: {.notes}
Absolute values are machine- and load-sensitive: run at rest and look for the
JUMPS, not the exact ns. Full sweep (8 KB → 64 MB) is in the notebook/script.
:::

## Why 6.5×? Bandwidth vs latency

- Table = wait for **one unpredictable** access (*latency*).
- Our loop reads **in order** → hardware loads next lines early.
- We pay the flow rate (**bandwidth**), not the wait.

. . .

> 100× is real when the next address is [**unpredictable**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} (linked list, random indices).

::: {.notes}
Not "the table is wrong" nor "machine noise". The part of the hardware that
loads lines early is the *prefetcher*. Latency and bandwidth are different
resources; a streaming sum is bandwidth-bound, a linked-list walk is latency-bound.
:::

## Two walks, same maths

. . .

Sum an 8000×8000 matrix, two loop orders:

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# COLUMN by column
for j in axes(M, 2)
    for i in axes(M, 1)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# ROW by row
for i in axes(M, 1)
    for j in axes(M, 2)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::::

- Julia: **column-major** (`M[i,j]`, `M[i+1,j]` adjacent).
- numpy: [**row-major**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}. Your reflexes are reversed.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "2. Locality — the same sum, walked two ways". Predict first.

## 11.9× for swapping two loops

. . .

8000² Float64 = 512 MB ≫ cache:

. . .

| walk | time | each 64 B line… |
|---|---|---|
| columns | **30.4 ms** | **fully used** (8 values) |
| rows | **361.4 ms** | **one** value, then evicted |

- Same result: [**11.9× slower**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.
- **Rule**: **first** index in the **inner** loop.

. . .

> Wrong order: right result, silently slow.

## Prove it's the cache 🔬

. . .

If Julia just "preferred columns", the gap would show at **any** size.

. . .

> ### Shrink the matrix. When does the gap vanish?

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Proof it IS the cache"

## Prove it's the cache — debrief

. . .

| size | footprint | rows / columns |
|---|---|---|
| 100² | 78 KB — **fits** | **0.9×** |
| 4000² | 122 MB — **spills** | **7.2×** |

- Gap appears **when data outgrows the cache**.

. . .

> Not "columns are fast": [**the cache decides**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

::: {.notes}
Small matrix: everything is already close, so the order cannot matter.
Strongest argument of the module: it rules out every explanation except the
cache. Pluto: interactive slider. Script: full table (100² → 4000²).
:::

## numpy hides it, doesn't remove it

. . .

C-order vs F-order arrays, 8000²:

. . .

| numpy | ratio | why |
|---|---|---|
| `A.sum(axis=0)` | **≈ 1×** | numpy **reorders** |
| copy F→C / C→C | **13.2×** (109.5 / 8.3 ms) | **can't** reorder a copy |

. . .

> [numpy hides it; Julia shows it. Neither removes it.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

::: {.notes}
On `sum`, someone wrote the reordering for you. A mismatched copy or a
hand-written loop: the full penalty is back.
Measured: sum(axis=0) C/F = 1.14× at 8000², 0.77× at 2000² — noise around 1×,
and load-sensitive (0.45× seen under load). Don't over-read either side of 1×.
Demo lives in the Python notebook (python/4).
:::

## Allocating is memory traffic too

. . .

```julia
z = 2 .* x .+ y      # NEW 76 MiB array
z .= 2 .* x .+ y     # reuses z
```

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Allocating is memory traffic too"

. . .

| n = 10⁷ | time | allocated |
|---|---|---|
| `z = …` | 54 ms | 76 MiB |
| `z .= …` | **17 ms** | [**0 bytes**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

. . .

> One dot: **~3×**. But **measure**: the gain isn't always there.

::: {.notes}
A new array is fresh memory to fetch and fill.
Same for BLAS: `A * B` allocates, `mul!(C, A, B)` reuses C. At n = 2000 on this
laptop the gain swings from no gain to ~3× from run to run (hybrid cores):
measure. numpy gains only ~1.4× with `out=`: it can't FUSE `2*x + y` into one
pass. For matrix × VECTOR the output is tiny and the gain vanishes. Measured at rest: mul!(y, W, x) on matrix-VECTOR was actually SLOWER than W * x
(760 vs 468 µs). On the GPU, in place gains nothing in Julia either (2.10 vs
1.82 ms; CUDA.jl allocates from a pool) — whereas torch in place does gain
(1.35 → 0.80 ms). The law is "allocation = memory traffic".
:::

# Part B — batching: memory-bound → compute-bound {style="text-align: center;"}

## Arithmetic intensity: FLOP per byte

. . .

| n×n, Float64 | FLOP | bytes | intensity |
|---|---|---|---|
| mat × **vec** | 2n² | 8n² | **0.25** — constant |
| mat × **mat** | 2n³ | 8n² | **n/4** — grows |

- **Low**: compute waits for loads → **memory-bound**.
- **High**: each value reused → **compute-bound**.

. . .

> Compare [**GFLOP/s**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}, not seconds.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "3. Arithmetic intensity"

::: {.notes}
Work per byte loaded; a FLOP = one `+` or `*`.
Don't compare seconds: they do different work. GFLOP/s = 10⁹ FLOP per second.
Intensity is per BYTE, not per value (8× apart for Float64) — be consistent.
BLAS-3 (GEMM) tiling is what realizes the n/4: each tile is reused from cache.
:::

## Batching = mat×vec → mat×mat

- A layer = matrix product. `W * x`: each weight used **once**.
- **B** examples as columns of `X`: `W * X` reuses each weight **B times**.

. . .

```julia
y = W * x     # 1 example
Y = W * X     # B examples
```

. . .

> [Not a GPU trick]{style="background-color: yellow;"}: it raises **intensity**. Must pay **on the CPU**.

## Batching on the CPU: bet 🎲

. . .

One layer `W` (4096² Float32), `B` examples as columns.

. . .

> ### What happens to the time **per example**?

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Batching: one layer W, B examples"

## Batching, measured on the CPU

. . .

| B | total | µs / example | GFLOP/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.55 ms | 2551.8 | 13.1 |
| 8 | 5.65 ms | 706.0 | 47.5 |
| 64 | 11.06 ms | 172.9 | 194.1 |
| 256 | 39.06 ms | 152.6 | 219.9 |
| 1024 | 141.80 ms | 138.5 | 242.3 |

. . .

> [**18.4×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} per example, 13.1 → 242.3 GFLOP/s. No GPU.

::: {.notes}
Same CPU, far more of it used. The GPU deck pushes the same idea further.
Honesty check (measured): B=1 here is a skinny GEMM (W * X[:,1:1]) at 2.55 ms;
a true gemv (W * x) is 1.09 ms — the B=1 baseline is 2.3× pessimistic. Against
the gemv baseline the per-example gain is still ~7.9×. Say it if asked.
numpy (python/4) gives almost the same numbers: 2101 → 113.6 µs (18.5×).
:::

## Why B = 1024 barely helps any more

. . .

2551.8 → 172.9 (B=64) → 152.6 (B=256) → 138.5 µs: **flattens**.

- `W` = **64 MiB** > **24 MiB L3**: a *fixed* RAM stream per batch.
- Batching divides it by B:

. . .

$$\text{time per example} \approx \text{compute} + \frac{\text{stream } W}{B}$$

- B ≈ 256: second term tiny.

. . .

> Flat = **success**: now compute-bound.

::: {.notes}
242 GFLOP/s is what this run reached, not the machine's peak. The 1/B model fits:
138.5 µs ≈ pure compute per example; 2551.8 ≈ that plus the whole W stream.
This is why python/4 uses n=4096: at 2000² W (16 MB) fits in L3 and the
mechanism disappears.
:::
